subject: Moses
note: Evidence for the Moses figure page. Every quotation is in moses.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs (142 printed, 128 entries). Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/moses/ (gitignored). The Bible is the Berean Standard Bible (public domain); the chapters quoted are copied into bsb-moses-chapters.txt with each chapter's verses run together on one line, so that a line crossing verses is found word for word. The 1916 Martyrology and the Fathers are the shared copies in sources/shared/.

life.text: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew son thrown into the Nile; Moses' mother hid him three months, set him in a papyrus basket among the reeds; Pharaoh's daughter found him, paid his own mother to nurse him, adopted and named him.
His parents were Amram and Jochebed, of Levi; Aaron was three years older (80 and 83 before Pharaoh); Miriam was their sister.
life.note: The sister of Exodus 2:4 is unnamed; Numbers 26:59 names the only sister Miriam.

life.text: Stephen splits his life into three forties: forty when he went out to his people, forty more before the bush, forty in the wilderness; he died at 120.
Stephen: "educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action".
Killing of the Egyptian, flight to Midian, the well, Zipporah, Gershom; Eliezer his second son; Jethro also called Reuel.
life.note: Numbers 12:1 speaks of a Cushite wife; the page says only that Numbers mentions one.

life.text: The bush, the Name, the objections, 'slow of speech and tongue', 'send someone else', Aaron as spokesman.
Before Pharaoh; straw withheld for the same quota of bricks; Moses' complaint to God.
The Passover, the death of the firstborn, about 600,000 men on foot besides women and children, 430 years in Egypt, Joseph's bones.

Amalek at Rephidim (hands held up by Aaron and Hur); Jethro's advice; Sinai in fire and smoke; forty days and nights twice; the tablets written by the finger of God, on both sides; the golden calf; the tent of meeting; the cleft of the rock; the shining face and the veil.
life.note: Paul's reading of the veil: 2 Corinthians 3:13-16.

life.text: Numbers: the cry for meat, the seventy elders, Eldad and Medad; Miriam and Aaron's complaint, 'a very humble man'; the spies and the forty years; Korah (Moses' first cousin); Meribah and the sentence on Moses and Aaron; Aaron's death on Mount Hor; the bronze snake; Joshua commissioned and renamed.
The Transfiguration: Moses and Elijah talking with Jesus about His departure (Greek exodos).
life.source: Luke 9:28-36; Matthew 17:1-8 (BSB); Strong's Greek 1841 at Bible Hub: 'exodos: Departure, Exodus'.

life.text: Dates: 1 Kings 6:1 read literally puts the Exodus about 1440 BC; Britannica prefers about 1290 BC, with Ramses II as the pharaoh of the Exodus; the king's name is not given.
life.source: Britannica, Moses (main page): 'One theory takes literally the statement in I Kings 6:1 ... the Exodus would date about 1440 bce'; 'the most probable date for the Exodus is about 1290 bce ... the pharaoh during the Exodus was Ramses II'; 'the personal name of the king is not given'.
life.note: The band's dates line, 'The 1400s or 1200s BC', gives both views.

life.text: The name: Josephus says Egyptian Mo (water) + Uses (saved); Britannica: from Egyptian mose, 'is born', as in Thutmose; the Catholic Encyclopedia gives the Hebrew mashah reading, Josephus's, and Lepsius's 'mesh (child)'.
life.source: Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 9 (Whiston); Britannica, Moses: 'the name Moses (Hebrew Moshe) is derived from Egyptian mose (“is born”) and is found in such names as Thutmose'; Catholic Encyclopedia, Moses, 'Name'.
life.note: Josephus also names Pharaoh's daughter Thermuthis (same chapter).

life.text: Hezekiah broke up the bronze snake, called Nehushtan, because Israel burned incense to it.
life.note: The first draft said 'about seven hundred years'; cut, because the interval depends on the disputed date of the Exodus.

life.text: Justin Martyr says Plato borrowed from Moses, 'the first prophet, and of greater antiquity than the Greek writers'.
life.note: 'about 155' is the usual date of the First Apology.

miracles.text: The ten plagues in order; the first (blood), the third (gnats, 'This is the finger of God'), the ninth (darkness, light in Israel's dwellings); the tenth in the Passover moment.
miracles.source: Exodus 7:14 to 12:32 (BSB): blood 7:20, frogs 8:2, gnats 8:16-19, flies 8:21, livestock 9:3, boils 9:9, hail 9:18, locusts 10:4, darkness 10:21-23, firstborn 12:29.
miracles.note: The magicians copied the first signs: Exodus 7:22; 8:7; they failed at the gnats: 8:18.

miracles.text: The sea (east wind, walls of water), manna (forty years), water from the rock at Horeb (Massah and Meribah), the bronze snake (John 3:14), Korah and the ground opening; Moses' pledge that it was 'not my own doing'.
Josephus tells the crossing 'as I found it in the sacred books', sets beside it the Pamphylian Sea's retreat before Alexander, and leaves it to the reader.

ten_commandments.text: No numbering in the text; the Jewish count makes Exodus 20:2 the first word and verses 3-6 one (the second); Philo and Josephus count verse 3 as i, verses 4-6 as ii; Catholics and Lutherans follow Augustine (Questions on Exodus 71), join 3-6 and split coveting; Josephus and Philo put five on each tablet; Rabbi Nehemiah said each held all ten.
ten_commandments.source: Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), Decalogue, 'Division of the Decalogue'; Josephus, Antiquities, book 3, chapter 5: 'five upon each table'.

ten_commandments.text: Catholic Encyclopedia: Augustine's count, 'adopted by the Council of Trent', 'followed also by the German Lutherans'; 'the English and Helvetian Protestant churches' follow Philo, Josephus, Origen.
ten_commandments.note: The page says 'the churches of England and Switzerland'.

ten_commandments.text: Luther's Small Catechism: the second commandment is the name of God. Westminster Shorter Catechism Q51: forbids 'the worshiping of God by images'. The Longer Catechism Q516-521: the second commandment is the graven image; honouring icons does not break it.
ten_commandments.source: Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 3 (Luther, Westminster) and vol. 2 (the Longer Catechism, tr. Blackmore), archive.org OCR.
ten_commandments.note: Q521's sentence runs on to 'icons are books'; the page stops before the OCR's line-break hyphen.

myths.text: Horns: Hebrew qaran, from qeren 'horn', 'send out rays' (BDB); Vulgate 'cornuta esset facies sua'; Douay-Rheims 'horned' with Challoner's note; Michelangelo's Moses, c. 1513-15, for the tomb of Julius II, San Pietro in Vincoli.
myths.source: Strong's Hebrew 7160 (BDB) at Bible Hub; The Latin Library, Exodus 34:29; drbo.org, Exodus 34:29 and note; Britannica, 'Moses, marble sculpture by Michelangelo for the tomb of Pope Julius II, c. 1513-15'.
myths.note: The horns on the statue are a matter of sight; Wikipedia (lead only) ties them to the Vulgate.

myths.text: Stutter: the Bible gives no cause; Acts 7:22 and Josephus praise his speech; the burning-coal legend and 'causing him to stutter' are the Jewish Encyclopedia's summary of Exodus Rabbah and medieval midrash.
myths.source: Exodus 4:10; Acts 7:22 (BSB); Josephus, Antiquities, book 4, chapter 8; Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), Moses: 'The angel Gabriel then guided his hand to the coal ... This burned his tongue, causing him to stutter (comp. Ex. iv. 10)'. Ginzberg, Legends of the Jews vol. 2 (1910), tells the same (fetched, not quoted).
myths.note: The page calls it 'a later Jewish legend, told in the Midrash' (the Jewish Encyclopedia cites Exodus Rabbah and later midrashic books); it gives no date.

myths.text: Red Sea / Sea of Reeds: suph = reeds, used for the Nile reeds of Exodus 2:3, 5; Britannica: 'Sea of Reeds (papyrus)', 'most probably a shallow lake in the far northeastern corner of Egypt', the Red Sea an 'erroneous interpretation'; Acts 7:36 and Hebrews 11:29 say Red Sea; 1 Kings 9:26 uses yam suph at Eloth; Catholic Encyclopedia: crossing 'at a point today unknown'.
myths.source: Strong's Hebrew 5488 (BDB and the occurrence list) at Bible Hub; Britannica, Moses, From Goshen to Sinai; Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), Moses; BSB.
myths.note: Britannica's main Moses page also carries an AI-written summary; nothing from it is used.

myths.text: Who wrote Deuteronomy 34: Philo (prophesied it), the Talmud (Joshua wrote the last eight verses / God dictated and Moses wrote in tears), Hobbes (1651, a later hand).
myths.source: Philo, On the Life of Moses II, 291 (Yonge); Babylonian Talmud, Baba Bathra, chapter 1 (fol. 14b-15a), tr. Rodkinson, at sacred-texts; Hobbes, Leviathan, chapter 33 (Gutenberg).

death.text: Nebo, Pisgah, the land shown; 'I have let you see it'; God buried him, grave unknown; 120, eyes not weak; thirty days of mourning; his plea to cross refused.

Jude 9: Michael and the devil over the body; Origen: from 'The Ascension of Moses'. Coptic synaxarium: God hid the body so Israel would not worship it. Josephus: a cloud, he disappeared, and wrote that he died 'out of fear'.
death.source: Jude 1:9 (BSB); Origen, De Principiis, book 3, chapter 2 (ANF 4, newadvent); CopticChurch.net, Synaxarium, 8 Tout; Josephus, Antiquities, book 4, chapter 8 (Whiston).

calendars.text: Roman Martyrology 1916, 4 September: 'On Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab, the holy lawgiver and prophet Moses.'
calendars.source: sources/shared/martyrology-1916.txt (the OCR reads the drop cap as 'AN' and puts a stray mark after 'holy'; quoted in two parts).

calendars.text: Litany of the Saints in the 1969 Calendarium Romanum: 'Sancte Moyses, ora pro nobis', under Patriarchs and Prophets. Moses has no day in the General Roman Calendar.
OCA: Holy Prophet and God-seer Moses, 4 September; the John Climacus story at Sinai.
calendars.note: The OCA prints 'Our Lord Moses'; the page prints 'Our lord Moses' (an honorific, not the Lord) so no reader mistakes it. The verifier ignores case.

calendars.text: Coptic: 8 Tout, the departure of Moses the Prophet. 1 Tout = 11 September (12 before a leap year), so 8 Tout = 18 (19) September.
calendars.source: CopticChurch.net, Synaxarium 8 Tout; wikipedia-coptic-calendar.txt (shared) for the date.

calendars.text: Lutheran (LCMS): Moses, 4 September. Not in the ELCA list, the Church of England's Common Worship calendar (only 'The Song of Moses and Miriam', a canticle) or Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022.

could_not_verify: The present Roman Martyrology (2004) entry for 4 September: not fetched; the page cites only the 1916 edition.
Greek and Russian Orthodox calendars: only the OCA was fetched. The 17 September line for churches on the old calendar is the 13-day arithmetic, as on Peter's page.
The date of the Rodkinson translation of Baba Bathra: not checked (sacred-texts' edition; Rodkinson died in 1904, so it is public domain).
The burning-coal legend's date: the Jewish Encyclopedia cites Exodus Rabbah and medieval books; the page calls it 'a later Jewish legend' and gives no date.
Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses: no public-domain English translation found, so nothing from it is used.

checker_2026_09_25.by: One light checking pass (Moses, Gideon, John the Baptist), 2026-09-25
checked: Every number against the BSB: 120 years and the three forties (Acts 7:23, 30, 36), 40 days twice (Exodus 24:18; 34:28), about 600,000 men and 430 years (Exodus 12:37, 40), 70 elders (Numbers 11), Aaron three years older (Exodus 7:7), Korah a first cousin (Exodus 6:18-21).
Dates: 1440 and 1290 BC as Britannica gives them; Justin about 155; Clement about 97; Josephus about 93; Michelangelo about 1513; Hobbes 1651.

Feasts read in the calendar texts: the 1916 Martyrology opens 4 September with Moses on Mount Nebo; "Sancte Moyses" in the 1969 Litany; LSB 4 September (its entry ends "The first five books of the Bible are attributed to him"); OCA 4 September; Coptic 8 Tout = 18 September (19 before a leap year); old calendar 17 September.

Attributions: the OCA story of John of the Ladder (read in oca-moses-life.txt); the Jewish Encyclopedia burning-coal legend (it cites Exodus Rabbah and later midrash); the Catholic Encyclopedia on the counts of the Commandments.

Disputes in each side's words with no winner: the Red Sea or Sea of Reeds, who wrote Deuteronomy 34, the four counts of the Ten Commandments. Josephus's disappearance story is labelled as his, as a later story.

Rules: capitals for God in our text and quotations; 'honoured as a saint', never 'St Moses'; no section marks; pictures' licences read on Commons (PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired; PD-Art); sizes match the data; band not violent; Doré's moses.jpg untouched.

changed: Ten Commandments, Reformed and Anglican: the Westminster Shorter Catechism put in italics, like the Small and Longer Catechisms beside it.
Is he a saint?, Catholic row: *Roman Martyrology* in italics (the italicize tool flagged it).
Stutter myth: the later legend now names where it is told ('a later Jewish legend, told in the Midrash'), from the Jewish Encyclopedia's own citation of Exodus Rabbah.
for_owner: The writer's open questions stand: the Ten Commandments section, the page's length (16 moments), Britannica's 'erroneous interpretation' in the Red Sea myth, Hobbes as the critic, and 'Our lord Moses' (the OCA prints 'Our Lord Moses'; the page lowers the capital so no reader takes it for God).
